7. Variance Reduction Techniques

Ways to get tighter confidence intervals from the same simulation budget: common random numbers, antithetic variates, control variates, indirect estimation, stratified sampling, conditioning, and importance sampling.

Estimate μ=E[X]\mu = \mathbf{E}[X]μ=E[X] from nnn i.i.d. replications X1,…,XnX_1, \dots, X_nX1​,…,Xn​: the point estimator is μ^=Xˉ(n)\hat\mu = \bar X(n)μ^​=Xˉ(n), and the 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\%100(1−α)% CI is

[μ^−tα/2, n−1σ2n,    μ^+tα/2, n−1σ2n ],σ2=Var⁡(X)\left[\hat\mu - t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n}},\;\; \hat\mu + t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}\,\right], \qquad \sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X) [μ^​−tα/2,n−1​nσ2​​,μ^​+tα/2,n−1​nσ2​​],σ2=Var(X)

(in practice σ2\sigma^2σ2 is estimated by S2(n)S^2(n)S2(n), as in §6.3).

Goal: reduce the variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 at no additional simulation cost. The half-width is proportional to σ/n\sigma/\sqrt nσ/n​, so there are two ways to make the CI narrower: more replications (a larger nnn, which costs computer time; by §6.3.3 the required nnn is proportional to σ2\sigma^2σ2), or a smaller σ2\sigma^2σ2 for the same nnn. Variance reduction techniques do the second, by using the random numbers more cleverly: halving σ2\sigma^2σ2 is as good as doubling nnn, but costs (almost) nothing.

7.1. Common Random Numbers (CRN)

Applicable when comparing two or more alternative systems.

Idea: we want the simulation experiments to be conducted under the same “experimental conditions”, i.e. with the same random numbers, so that an observed difference in performance is due to the difference between the systems and not to the random numbers (“luck”) of each simulation.

Ex: 1. M/M/1, 2. M/M/2.

XiX_iXi​ = average delay in queue in system i=1,2i = 1, 2i=1,2. Goal: estimate ζ=E[Z]=E[X1−X2]\zeta = \mathbf{E}[Z] = \mathbf{E}[X_1 - X_2]ζ=E[Z]=E[X1​−X2​], where Z=X1−X2Z = X_1 - X_2Z=X1​−X2​.

Repeat the experiment nnn times (each time simulating both systems) and get Z1,Z2,…,ZnZ_1, Z_2, \dots, Z_nZ1​,Z2​,…,Zn​, with Zj=X1j−X2jZ_j = X_{1j} - X_{2j}Zj​=X1j​−X2j​. The point estimator is

Zˉ(n)=1n∑j=1nZj,\bar Z(n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n Z_j , Zˉ(n)=n1​j=1∑n​Zj​,

and the half-width of the 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\%100(1−α)% CI is

tα/2, n−1Var⁡(Z1)nt_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)}{n}} tα/2,n−1​nVar(Z1​)​​

(with Var⁡(Z1)\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)Var(Z1​) estimated by the sample variance of the ZjZ_jZj​’s), where

Var⁡(Z1)=Var⁡(X1−X2)=Var⁡(X1)+Var⁡(X2)−2cov⁡(X1,X2).\operatorname{Var}(Z_1) = \operatorname{Var}(X_1 - X_2) = \operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{Var}(X_2) - 2\operatorname{cov}(X_1, X_2) . Var(Z1​)=Var(X1​−X2​)=Var(X1​)+Var(X2​)−2cov(X1​,X2​).

If the two systems are simulated with independent random numbers, cov⁡(X1,X2)=0\operatorname{cov}(X_1, X_2) = 0cov(X1​,X2​)=0. We want cov⁡(X1,X2)>0\operatorname{cov}(X_1, X_2) > 0cov(X1​,X2​)>0: then the last term is subtracted and Var⁡(Z1)\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)Var(Z1​) is smaller than with independent sampling.

CRN is a technique that tries to induce this positive correlation by using the same random numbers to simulate all alternative systems. (A first example was in §6.3.3: for M/M/1 vs M/D/1, CRN reduced Var⁡(Zj)\operatorname{Var}(Z_j)Var(Zj​) from 3.79 to 2.23.)

When does CRN work?

u1,u2,…,un  ⟶  simulation program  ⟶  Xu_1, u_2, \dots, u_n \;\longrightarrow\; \boxed{\text{simulation program}} \;\longrightarrow\; X u1​,u2​,…,un​⟶simulation program​⟶X

The simulation program is a (complicated, but deterministic) function of the random numbers: X=X(u1,u2,… )X = X(u_1, u_2, \dots)X=X(u1​,u2​,…). To picture it, pretend that XXX depends on a single random number: X=X(u)X = X(u)X=X(u). CRN feeds the same uuu to both systems, so the question is how X1(u)X_1(u)X1​(u) and X2(u)X_2(u)X2​(u) react to uuu.

Desired cases: X1X_1X1​ and X2X_2X2​ both increase, or both decrease, in uuu.

Backfire: one increases while the other decreases. Then CRN induces a negative correlation and increases the variance.

How can we guarantee the desired case? There is no guarantee: the simulation program is far too complicated to check whether it is monotone in every random number. But we can make it very likely, by looking at the two parts that turn random numbers into an output:

flowchart LR
    U(["uᵢ's"]) --> RVG
    subgraph H["X(u₁, u₂, …): monotone if each box is monotone"]
        RVG["RVG: random numbers → random variates"] --> SP["simulation program: random variates → X"]
    end
    SP --> X(["X"])

The composition of two monotone functions is also monotone, so each part has to be monotone:

  • The random variate generator (RVG) is under our control. Use the inverse transform (§4.2.1): X=F−1(u)X = F^{-1}(u)X=F−1(u) is increasing in uuu, so a larger uuu always gives a larger variate. Other methods are not monotone; e.g. with acceptance–rejection a slightly different uuu can change which candidate is accepted, and even how many uuu’s are used. So always use the inverse transform in the CRN approach.
  • The simulation program (the model itself) should react monotonically to the variates. This we cannot control, but it can usually be checked by reasoning about the model, as in the queueing example below.

Queueing simulation (service times in the M/M/1 and the M/M/2 system, both generated by the inverse transform from the same uuu):

u↑  ⇒  S1↑ and S2↑  ⇒  X1↑ and X2↑u \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; S_1 \uparrow \text{ and } S_2 \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; X_1 \uparrow \text{ and } X_2 \uparrow u↑⇒S1​↑ and S2​↑⇒X1​↑ and X2​↑

(longer service times mean longer delays in both systems). Likewise for interarrival times: u↑⇒A1↑u \uparrow \Rightarrow A_1 \uparrowu↑⇒A1​↑ and A2↑⇒X1↓A_2 \uparrow \Rightarrow X_1 \downarrowA2​↑⇒X1​↓ and X2↓X_2 \downarrowX2​↓. Both systems react in the same direction to every random number, which is the desired case.

Synchronization: it is not enough to use the same stream of random numbers to simulate the alternative systems. We must match up (synchronize) the random numbers across the different systems, to ensure that the same uuu is used for the same purpose in the different systems.

Ex: one stream u1,u2,…u_1, u_2, \dotsu1​,u2​,… is used for everything, each random number being taken when the program needs one (A = used for an interarrival time, S = used for a service time):

random number used in M/M/1 for used in M/M/2 for
u1u_1u1​ A A
u2u_2u2​ A A
⋮\vdots⋮ ⋮\vdots⋮ ⋮\vdots⋮
u7u_7u7​ S S
u8u_8u8​ A A
→u9\to u_9→u9​ A S

Up to u8u_8u8​ the two systems happen to need the random numbers for the same purposes. But the systems are different, so their events eventually happen in a different order: e.g. in the M/M/2 system a waiting customer starts service on the second server (which needs a service time) while in the M/M/1 system the next event is an arrival (which needs an interarrival time). From u9u_9u9​ on, the same uuu is used as an interarrival time in one system and as a service time in the other, and all later random numbers are shifted as well. The two systems are no longer driven by the same inputs, and most of the positive correlation is lost.

General synchronization methods:

  • Dedicate a stream of random numbers to a particular source of randomness (§3.3), e.g. stream 1 for all interarrival times and stream 2 for all service times. Then the kkk-th interarrival time always uses the kkk-th number of stream 1, in both systems, no matter in which order the events happen.
  • Use the inverse transform method to generate random variates: it guarantees monotonicity and is one-to-one (exactly one uuu per variate). With acceptance–rejection, the number of uuu’s used per variate is random, so the streams drift out of synchronization even when they are dedicated.
  • Generate all random variates beforehand, e.g. generate customer jjj’s service time when customer jjj arrives and attach it to the customer. Then customer jjj has the same service time in both systems, even if it starts service at different times or (with other queue disciplines) in a different order.

E.g. with numbers (my choice): arrival rate 1; system 1 has one server with mean service time 0.9, system 2 has two servers with mean service time 1.8 each (the same total capacity); XiX_iXi​ = average delay in queue of the first 100 customers, starting empty; 3000 replications of each version:

random numbers corr⁡(X1,X2)\operatorname{corr}(X_1, X_2)corr(X1​,X2​) Var⁡(Z)\operatorname{Var}(Z)Var(Z) change
independent for the two systems 0.01 16.4
CRN, one shared stream, not synchronized 0.08 15.7 −4%
CRN, dedicated streams for arrivals and services (synchronized) 0.997 0.057 −99.7%
backfire: system 2 uses 1−u1 - u1−u wherever system 1 uses uuu −0.36 23.3 +42%

Here E[Z]≈0.43\mathbf{E}[Z] \approx 0.43E[Z]≈0.43 (the M/M/2 system has slightly shorter delays). With n=10n = 10n=10 replications, the 95% CI half-width is 2.26216.4/10=2.92.262\sqrt{16.4/10} = 2.92.26216.4/10​=2.9 with independent random numbers (the CI cannot even tell which system is better), but 2.2620.057/10=0.172.262\sqrt{0.057/10} = 0.172.2620.057/10​=0.17 with synchronized CRN. Note that sharing a stream without synchronization gives almost nothing: CRN only works when the same uuu is used for the same purpose.

7.2. Antithetic Variates (AV)

Used when investigating the performance of a single system.

Idea: make the replications in pairs, such that a large observation in the first replication of a pair tends to be matched by a small one in the second; their average is then closer to μ\muμ than the average of two independent replications.

  • Use uiu_iui​’s for the first replication of a pair to get X(1)X^{(1)}X(1).
  • Use 1−ui1 - u_i1−ui​’s for the second replication, in the same roles, to get X(2)X^{(2)}X(2).

Since 1−U∼U(0,1)1 - U \sim U(0, 1)1−U∼U(0,1) when U∼U(0,1)U \sim U(0, 1)U∼U(0,1), both are valid replications: E[X(1)]=E[X(2)]=μ\mathbf{E}[X^{(1)}] = \mathbf{E}[X^{(2)}] = \muE[X(1)]=E[X(2)]=μ and Var⁡(X(1))=Var⁡(X(2))=σ2\operatorname{Var}(X^{(1)}) = \operatorname{Var}(X^{(2)}) = \sigma^2Var(X(1))=Var(X(2))=σ2. (X(1),X(2)X^{(1)}, X^{(2)}X(1),X(2) are the two runs of one pair, not two systems as in §7.1.) Use the pair average as the observation:

X=X(1)+X(2)2,E[X]=μ,X = \frac{X^{(1)} + X^{(2)}}{2}, \qquad \mathbf{E}[X] = \mu, X=2X(1)+X(2)​,E[X]=μ,

Var⁡(X)=14[Var⁡(X(1))+Var⁡(X(2))+2cov⁡(X(1),X(2))]=σ2+cov⁡(X(1),X(2))2.\operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{4}\Big[\operatorname{Var}(X^{(1)}) + \operatorname{Var}(X^{(2)}) + 2\operatorname{cov}(X^{(1)}, X^{(2)})\Big] = \frac{\sigma^2 + \operatorname{cov}(X^{(1)}, X^{(2)})}{2} . Var(X)=41​[Var(X(1))+Var(X(2))+2cov(X(1),X(2))]=2σ2+cov(X(1),X(2))​.

With two independent replications the covariance would be 0 and the variance σ2/2\sigma^2/2σ2/2. So AV helps exactly when cov⁡(X(1),X(2))<0\operatorname{cov}(X^{(1)}, X^{(2)}) < 0cov(X(1),X(2))<0. With nnn pairs (different pairs use independent random numbers), the pair averages X1,…,XnX_1, \dots, X_nX1​,…,Xn​ are i.i.d., and the CI is computed from them as usual, with tα/2, n−1t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}tα/2,n−1​.

Why the covariance is negative:

ui↑  ⇒  X(1)↑,1−ui↓  ⇒  X(2)↓.u_i \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; X^{(1)} \uparrow, \qquad 1 - u_i \downarrow \;\Rightarrow\; X^{(2)} \downarrow . ui​↑⇒X(1)↑,1−ui​↓⇒X(2)↓.

Applicability: the output reacts monotonically to the underlying random numbers (the same condition as for CRN; here it makes the two runs of a pair move in opposite directions).

Practical issues:

  • Synchronization: 1−ui1 - u_i1−ui​ must be used for exactly the same purpose in the second run as uiu_iui​ in the first.
  • Use the inverse transform to generate random variates (monotone, one uuu per variate).
  • Use dedicated streams for the different sources of randomness.
  • Do not combine CRN with AV (in a comparison of systems): it may backfire. With both, system 1’s first run (with uuu) and system 2’s second run (with 1−u1 - u1−u) are negatively correlated, and these cross-covariances enter Var⁡(Z)\operatorname{Var}(Z)Var(Z) with the wrong sign: they increase it. Whether the net effect is a reduction is not clear in advance.

Ex: θ=E[eU]\theta = \mathbf{E}[e^U]θ=E[eU], U∼U(0,1)U \sim U(0, 1)U∼U(0,1):

θ=∫01eu⋅1 du=e−1=1.718.\theta = \int_0^1 e^u \cdot 1\, du = e - 1 = 1.718 . θ=∫01​eu⋅1du=e−1=1.718.

7.3. Control Variates (CV)

Goal: estimate μ=E[X]\mu = \mathbf{E}[X]μ=E[X], XXX = average delay in queue of the first 100 customers.

Suppose there is an intermediate r.v. YYY satisfying

  1. the value of YYY can be observed (in the same run as XXX);
  2. YYY and XXX are correlated;
  3. ν=E[Y]\nu = \mathbf{E}[Y]ν=E[Y] is known.

E.g. YYY = average service time of the first 99 customers. ν\nuν is known: it is the mean of the service-time distribution, which we chose as an input. (99, not 100: the delays of customers 1,…,1001, \dots, 1001,…,100 depend only on the service times of customers 1,…,991, \dots, 991,…,99.)

If Y>νY > \nuY>ν (the service times happened to be long in this run) ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ probably X>μX > \muX>μ (the delays are long too) ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ adjust the value of XXX downwards, towards μ\muμ.

If Y<νY < \nuY<ν ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ probably X<μX < \muX<μ ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ adjust XXX upwards.

YYY is called a control variate: it measures how lucky or unlucky the run was, and we correct XXX for that luck.

How to decide the adjustment amount?

Let XXX = the observed value and XcX_cXc​ = the value of XXX after the adjustment, so the adjustment amount is X−XcX - X_cX−Xc​. Assume it is proportional to how far YYY is from its mean:

X−Xc=a(Y−ν),Xc=X−a(Y−ν).X - X_c = a(Y - \nu), \qquad X_c = X - a(Y - \nu). X−Xc​=a(Y−ν),Xc​=X−a(Y−ν).

E[Xc]=E[X]−a E[Y−ν]=μ−a⋅0=μ,\mathbf{E}[X_c] = \mathbf{E}[X] - a\,\mathbf{E}[Y - \nu] = \mu - a \cdot 0 = \mu, E[Xc​]=E[X]−aE[Y−ν]=μ−a⋅0=μ,

so XcX_cXc​ is unbiased for every constant aaa. Its variance (ν\nuν is a constant, so it does not affect the variance):

Var⁡(Xc)=Var⁡(X−aY)=Var⁡(X)+{a2Var⁡(Y)−2acov⁡(X,Y)}⏟want ≤ 0.\operatorname{Var}(X_c) = \operatorname{Var}(X - aY) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \underbrace{\big\{a^2\operatorname{Var}(Y) - 2a\operatorname{cov}(X, Y)\big\}}_{\text{want } \le\, 0} . Var(Xc​)=Var(X−aY)=Var(X)+want ≤0{a2Var(Y)−2acov(X,Y)}​​.

Var⁡(Xc)≤Var⁡(X)\operatorname{Var}(X_c) \le \operatorname{Var}(X)Var(Xc​)≤Var(X) exactly when the term in braces is ≤0\le 0≤0.

If a=1a = 1a=1, then YYY should be chosen such that Var⁡(Y)≤2cov⁡(X,Y)\operatorname{Var}(Y) \le 2\operatorname{cov}(X, Y)Var(Y)≤2cov(X,Y).

Idea: find the a∗a^*a∗ such that Var⁡(Xc)\operatorname{Var}(X_c)Var(Xc​) is minimized:

dVar⁡(Xc)da=2aVar⁡(Y)−2cov⁡(X,Y)=0⇒a∗=cov⁡(X,Y)Var⁡(Y)\frac{d\operatorname{Var}(X_c)}{da} = 2a\operatorname{Var}(Y) - 2\operatorname{cov}(X, Y) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad a^* = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X, Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} dadVar(Xc​)​=2aVar(Y)−2cov(X,Y)=0⇒a∗=Var(Y)cov(X,Y)​

(the slope of the least-squares line of XXX on YYY, the line in the figure above). The control-variate estimator is then

Idea: use known relationships, and replace random quantities by constant known quantities wherever possible.

Little’s Law

L=λ⋅wL = \lambda \cdot w L=λ⋅w

where λ\lambdaλ is the arrival rate; likewise LQ=λ⋅dL_Q = \lambda \cdot dLQ​=λ⋅d.

Why: each customer is charged 1 dollar for every unit of time he spends in the system. Compute the long-run average reward earned per unit time in two ways:

  • By time: at time ttt, L(t)L(t)L(t) customers are in the system, each paying 1 dollar per unit time, so the reward rate is L(t)L(t)L(t). The total reward up to time TTT is ∫0TL(t) dt\int_0^T L(t)\, dt∫0T​L(t)dt, and the average reward per unit time is 1T∫0TL(t) dt→L\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T L(t)\, dt \to LT1​∫0T​L(t)dt→L.
  • By customer: customer iii pays WiW_iWi​ in total. With N(T)N(T)N(T) = the number of customers who arrived by time TTT,

1T∑i=1N(T)Wi=N(T)T⋅1N(T)∑i=1N(T)Wi  →  λ⋅w,\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{N(T)} W_i = \frac{N(T)}{T}\cdot\frac{1}{N(T)}\sum_{i=1}^{N(T)} W_i \;\to\; \lambda \cdot w, T1​i=1∑N(T)​Wi​=TN(T)​⋅N(T)1​i=1∑N(T)​Wi​→λ⋅w,

since N(T)/T→λN(T)/T \to \lambdaN(T)/T→λ (arrivals per unit time) and the average of the WiW_iWi​’s →w\to w→w. (Customers still in the system at time TTT have not paid everything yet, but this is negligible as T→∞T \to \inftyT→∞.)

Both compute the same long-run reward rate, so L=λwL = \lambda wL=λw. Charging only for the time spent in the queue gives LQ=λdL_Q = \lambda dLQ​=λd in the same way.

So all four quantities are estimated from d^(n)\hat d(n)d^(n) alone.

Var⁡(g^)=12n[A2+B2−(A+B)2],\operatorname{Var}(\hat g) = \frac{1}{2n}\big[A_2 + B_2 - (A + B)^2\big], Var(g^​)=2n1​[A2​+B2​−(A+B)2],

Var⁡(g^)−Var⁡(g~)=12n[2A2+2B2−(A+B)2]=12n(A−B)2≥0.\operatorname{Var}(\hat g) - \operatorname{Var}(\tilde g) = \frac{1}{2n}\big[2A^2 + 2B^2 - (A + B)^2\big] = \frac{1}{2n}(A - B)^2 \ge 0 . Var(g^​)−Var(g~​)=2n1​[2A2+2B2−(A+B)2]=2n1​(A−B)2≥0.

The reduction is large when the two halves have very different integrals. Crude Monte Carlo may by chance put more points in one half; stratification puts exactly nnn in each:

E.g. g(x)=exg(x) = e^xg(x)=ex: A=e1/2−1=0.649A = e^{1/2} - 1 = 0.649A=e1/2−1=0.649, B=e−e1/2=1.070B = e - e^{1/2} = 1.070B=e−e1/2=1.070, (A−B)2=0.177(A - B)^2 = 0.177(A−B)2=0.177, and Var⁡(g(U))=0.242\operatorname{Var}(g(U)) = 0.242Var(g(U))=0.242. So Var⁡(g^)=0.242/2n\operatorname{Var}(\hat g) = 0.242/2nVar(g^​)=0.242/2n and Var⁡(g~)=(0.242−0.177)/2n=0.065/2n\operatorname{Var}(\tilde g) = (0.242 - 0.177)/2n = 0.065/2nVar(g~​)=(0.242−0.177)/2n=0.065/2n: a 73% reduction.

7.6. Conditioning

Goal: estimate μ=E[X]\mu = \mathbf{E}[X]μ=E[X], using an intermediate r.v. ZZZ satisfying: if the value of ZZZ is known, then E[X∣Z=z]\mathbf{E}[X \mid Z = z]E[X∣Z=z] is a known, deterministic function of zzz (it can be computed exactly, without simulation).

μ=E[X]=E[E[X∣Z]].\mu = \mathbf{E}[X] = \mathbf{E}\big[\mathbf{E}[X \mid Z]\big] . μ=E[X]=E[E[X∣Z]].

The conditioning estimator is

μ^=E[X∣Z=z],\hat\mu = \mathbf{E}[X \mid Z = z], μ^​=E[X∣Z=z],

evaluated at the observed value zzz of ZZZ (i.e. the random variable E[X∣Z]\mathbf{E}[X \mid Z]E[X∣Z]): instead of using the observed XXX, observe ZZZ and use the exact conditional mean.

Ex: a single-server queue (FCFS) with exponential service times. μ=E[Di]\mu = \mathbf{E}[D_i]μ=E[Di​], DiD_iDi​ = delay of the iii-th customer. ZZZ = number of customers in the system seen by the iii-th arrival. Then

E[Di∣Z=z]=z E[S].\mathbf{E}[D_i \mid Z = z] = z\,\mathbf{E}[S] . E[Di​∣Z=z]=zE[S].

Why: customer iii has to wait for the zzz customers ahead of him. The z−1z - 1z−1 customers waiting in the queue each need a full service time (mean E[S]\mathbf{E}[S]E[S]). The customer in service needs its remaining service time, which by the memoryless property of the exponential distribution also has mean E[S]\mathbf{E}[S]E[S], no matter how long the service has already lasted. In total, z E[S]z\,\mathbf{E}[S]zE[S]. (With non-exponential service times the remaining service time would depend on the elapsed service time, and the formula would fail.) So the conditioning estimator of E[Di]\mathbf{E}[D_i]E[Di​] is Z E[S]Z\,\mathbf{E}[S]ZE[S], and for the average delay of the first nnn customers it is 1n∑i=1nZi E[S]\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\,\mathbf{E}[S]n1​∑i=1n​Zi​E[S].

Law of total variance:

Var⁡(X)=E[Var⁡(X∣Z)]+Var⁡(E[X∣Z])\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbf{E}\big[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)\big] + \operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbf{E}[X \mid Z]\big) Var(X)=E[Var(X∣Z)]+Var(E[X∣Z])

(total variance = average variance within each value of ZZZ + variance of the conditional means). Hence

Var⁡(E[X∣Z])=Var⁡(X)−E[Var⁡(X∣Z)]≤Var⁡(X),\operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbf{E}[X \mid Z]\big) = \operatorname{Var}(X) - \mathbf{E}\big[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)\big] \le \operatorname{Var}(X), Var(E[X∣Z])=Var(X)−E[Var(X∣Z)]≤Var(X),

since E[Var⁡(X∣Z)]≥0\mathbf{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)] \ge 0E[Var(X∣Z)]≥0. So the conditioning estimator μ^=E[X∣Z]\hat\mu = \mathbf{E}[X \mid Z]μ^​=E[X∣Z] is unbiased (because μ=E[X]=E[E[X∣Z]]\mu = \mathbf{E}[X] = \mathbf{E}[\mathbf{E}[X \mid Z]]μ=E[X]=E[E[X∣Z]]) and its variance is never larger than that of XXX. The randomness it removes is E[Var⁡(X∣Z)]\mathbf{E}[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)]E[Var(X∣Z)]: here, the randomness of the actual service times of the customers ahead, which is averaged out exactly instead of being simulated.

E.g. M/M/1 queue (λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1, E[S]=0.9\mathbf{E}[S] = 0.9E[S]=0.9, empty start), XXX = average delay of the first 100 customers (20,000 runs): both estimators have mean 4.13, but Var⁡(X)=8.48\operatorname{Var}(X) = 8.48Var(X)=8.48 while Var⁡(1100∑i0.9 Zi)=6.56\operatorname{Var}\big(\frac{1}{100}\sum_i 0.9\,Z_i\big) = 6.56Var(1001​∑i​0.9Zi​)=6.56, a 23% reduction.

7.7. Importance Sampling

Goal: estimate

μ=E[X]=E[h(Y)]=∫−∞∞h(y)f(y) dy=∫−∞∞h(y) f(y)g(y) g(y) dy,\mu = \mathbf{E}[X] = \mathbf{E}[h(Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(y) f(y)\, dy = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(y)\,\frac{f(y)}{g(y)}\, g(y)\, dy, μ=E[X]=E[h(Y)]=∫−∞∞​h(y)f(y)dy=∫−∞∞​h(y)g(y)f(y)​g(y)dy,

where YYY has density fff, and ggg is another density that we choose (and can sample from). We need fff to be absolutely continuous with respect to ggg (the board said “ggg with respect to fff”, but the “i.e.” part is the right condition), i.e. whenever g(y)=0g(y) = 0g(y)=0, f(y)=0f(y) = 0f(y)=0. Equivalently:

support of f⊆support of g,\text{support of } f \subseteq \text{support of } g, support of f⊆support of g,

where the support of fff is the set of values of yyy s.t. f(y)>0f(y) > 0f(y)>0.
Why this is needed: we divide by g(y)g(y)g(y), and any region where f(y)>0f(y) > 0f(y)>0 but g(y)=0g(y) = 0g(y)=0 would never be sampled from ggg, so that part of the integral would be missed. (Strictly, it is enough where h(y)≠0h(y) \ne 0h(y)=0.)

Write Ef\mathbf{E}_fEf​ for an expectation when YYY has density fff, and Eg\mathbf{E}_gEg​ when YYY has density ggg. Then

μ=E[X]=Eg ⁣[h(Y) f(Y)g(Y)].\mu = \mathbf{E}[X] = \mathbf{E}_g\!\left[h(Y)\,\frac{f(Y)}{g(Y)}\right]. μ=E[X]=Eg​[h(Y)g(Y)f(Y)​].

Generate Y1,Y2,…,Yn∼gY_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_n \sim gY1​,Y2​,…,Yn​∼g (i.i.d.) and use

μ^(n)=1n∑i=1nh(Yi){f(Yi)g(Yi)}⏟likelihood ratio.\hat\mu(n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n h(Y_i)\underbrace{\left\{\frac{f(Y_i)}{g(Y_i)}\right\}}_{\text{likelihood ratio}} . μ^​(n)=n1​i=1∑n​h(Yi​)likelihood ratio{g(Yi​)f(Yi​)​}​​.

This one is unbiased, Eg[μ^(n)]=μ\mathbf{E}_g[\hat\mu(n)] = \muEg​[μ^​(n)]=μ, just like the crude estimator 1n∑i=1nh(Yi)\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n h(Y_i)n1​∑i=1n​h(Yi​) with Yi∼fY_i \sim fYi​∼f. The likelihood ratio is a weight that corrects for sampling from the “wrong” density: values that ggg produces more often than fff would (g>fg > fg>f) get weight <1< 1<1, values that ggg produces less often get weight >1> 1>1.

Variance:

Var⁡(μ^(n))=1n(Eg ⁣[h2(Y)f2(Y)g2(Y)]−{Eg ⁣[h(Y)f(Y)g(Y)]}2⏟= μ2)=1n Eg ⁣[h2(Y)f2(Y)g2(Y)]−1nμ2=1n∫h2(y)f2(y)g2(y) g(y) dy−1nμ2=1n∫h2(y)f2(y)g(y) dy−1nμ2(one g(y) cancels)=1n∫h2(y) f(y)g(y) f(y) dy−1nμ2=1n Ef ⁣[h2(Y)f(Y)g(Y)]−1nμ2.\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu(n)) &= \frac{1}{n}\left(\mathbf{E}_g\!\left[\frac{h^2(Y)f^2(Y)}{g^2(Y)}\right] - \underbrace{\left\{\mathbf{E}_g\!\left[\frac{h(Y)f(Y)}{g(Y)}\right]\right\}^2}_{=\ \mu^2}\right) \\ &= \frac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{E}_g\!\left[\frac{h^2(Y)f^2(Y)}{g^2(Y)}\right] - \frac{1}{n}\mu^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{n}\int \frac{h^2(y)f^2(y)}{g^2(y)}\, g(y)\, dy - \frac{1}{n}\mu^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{n}\int \frac{h^2(y)f^2(y)}{g(y)}\, dy - \frac{1}{n}\mu^2 \qquad (\text{one } g(y) \text{ cancels}) \\ &= \frac{1}{n}\int h^2(y)\,\frac{f(y)}{g(y)}\, f(y)\, dy - \frac{1}{n}\mu^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{E}_f\!\left[\frac{h^2(Y)f(Y)}{g(Y)}\right] - \frac{1}{n}\mu^2 . \end{aligned} Var(μ^​(n))​=n1​​Eg​[g2(Y)h2(Y)f2(Y)​]−= μ2{Eg​[g(Y)h(Y)f(Y)​]}2​​​=n1​Eg​[g2(Y)h2(Y)f2(Y)​]−n1​μ2=n1​∫g2(y)h2(y)f2(y)​g(y)dy−n1​μ2=n1​∫g(y)h2(y)f2(y)​dy−n1​μ2(one g(y) cancels)=n1​∫h2(y)g(y)f(y)​f(y)dy−n1​μ2=n1​Ef​[g(Y)h2(Y)f(Y)​]−n1​μ2.​

“Y∼fY \sim fY∼f? Wait, but YYY is already ∼g\sim g∼g?” In the simulation, the YiY_iYi​’s are always generated from ggg; nothing changes there. The subscript of E\mathbf{E}E only says which density the integral is taken against: Eg[k(Y)]=∫k(y)g(y) dy\mathbf{E}_g[k(Y)] = \int k(y) g(y)\, dyEg​[k(Y)]=∫k(y)g(y)dy and Ef[k(Y)]=∫k(y)f(y) dy\mathbf{E}_f[k(Y)] = \int k(y) f(y)\, dyEf​[k(Y)]=∫k(y)f(y)dy, and the YYY inside is just a name for the integration variable. The last step does not change the number: it regroups the same integral ∫h2f2/g dy\int h^2 f^2/g\, dy∫h2f2/gdy, using f(y)f(y)f(y) instead of g(y)g(y)g(y) as the density, so that it can be compared with crude Monte Carlo:

crude (Yi∼f):  Var⁡=1n Ef[h2(Y)]−1nμ2,\text{crude } (Y_i \sim f):\ \ \operatorname{Var} = \frac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{E}_f\big[h^2(Y)\big] - \frac{1}{n}\mu^2, crude (Yi​∼f):  Var=n1​Ef​[h2(Y)]−n1​μ2,

importance sampling (Yi∼g):  Var⁡=1n Ef ⁣[h2(Y) f(Y)g(Y)]−1nμ2.\text{importance sampling } (Y_i \sim g):\ \ \operatorname{Var} = \frac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{E}_f\!\left[h^2(Y)\,\frac{f(Y)}{g(Y)}\right] - \frac{1}{n}\mu^2 . importance sampling (Yi​∼g):  Var=n1​Ef​[h2(Y)g(Y)f(Y)​]−n1​μ2.

The μ2\mu^2μ2 terms are the same, so importance sampling wins when f(y)/g(y)<1f(y)/g(y) < 1f(y)/g(y)<1 mostly where h2(y)f(y)h^2(y) f(y)h2(y)f(y) is large: ggg should generate the “important” values (those that contribute most to the integral) more often than fff does. Hence the name.

Choosing ggg: only the first term depends on ggg, so we want

min⁡g Ef ⁣[h2(Y)f(Y)g(Y)].\min_g\ \mathbf{E}_f\!\left[\frac{h^2(Y)f(Y)}{g(Y)}\right]. gmin​ Ef​[g(Y)h2(Y)f(Y)​].

  • The best possible choice (for h≥0h \ge 0h≥0) is g∗(y)=h(y)f(y)/μg^*(y) = h(y)f(y)/\mug∗(y)=h(y)f(y)/μ: then h(y)f(y)/g∗(y)=μh(y)f(y)/g^*(y) = \muh(y)f(y)/g∗(y)=μ for every yyy and the variance is 0. It cannot be used, because it requires the unknown μ\muμ, but it is the guideline: choose ggg roughly proportional to h⋅fh \cdot fh⋅f.
  • In practice, ggg is chosen from a family and its parameter is optimized. E.g. if fff is Exp(λ)\text{Exp}(\lambda)Exp(λ), take g=Exp(λ′)g = \text{Exp}(\lambda')g=Exp(λ′) and choose the rate λ′\lambda'λ′. (The board called this rate μ\muμ; I renamed it to avoid a clash with μ=E[X]\mu = \mathbf{E}[X]μ=E[X].)

Ex (worked out for this family): estimate p=P(Y>a)p = P(Y > a)p=P(Y>a) for Y∼Exp(λ)Y \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)Y∼Exp(λ), so h(y)=I{y>a}h(y) = I\{y > a\}h(y)=I{y>a} (the indicator III is explained in the next example). For λ′<2λ\lambda' < 2\lambdaλ′<2λ,

Ef ⁣[h2(Y)f(Y)g(Y)]=∫a∞(λe−λy)2λ′e−λ′y dy=λ2 e−(2λ−λ′)aλ′(2λ−λ′),\mathbf{E}_f\!\left[\frac{h^2(Y)f(Y)}{g(Y)}\right] = \int_a^\infty \frac{(\lambda e^{-\lambda y})^2}{\lambda' e^{-\lambda' y}}\, dy = \frac{\lambda^2\, e^{-(2\lambda - \lambda')a}}{\lambda'(2\lambda - \lambda')}, Ef​[g(Y)h2(Y)f(Y)​]=∫a∞​λ′e−λ′y(λe−λy)2​dy=λ′(2λ−λ′)λ2e−(2λ−λ′)a​,

and setting the derivative of its logarithm to 0 gives

λ′∗=λ+1a−λ2+1a2  ≈  1afor large a,\lambda'^* = \lambda + \frac{1}{a} - \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \frac{1}{a^2}} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{a} \quad \text{for large } a, λ′∗=λ+a1​−λ2+a21​​≈a1​for large a,

i.e. the best ggg has mean ≈a\approx a≈a: it puts the samples around the threshold. With λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 and a=20a = 20a=20, p=e−20=2.06×10−9p = e^{-20} = 2.06 \times 10^{-9}p=e−20=2.06×10−9. One crude sample has standard deviation p(1−p)≈22,000×p\sqrt{p(1-p)} \approx 22{,}000 \times pp(1−p)​≈22,000×p. One importance sample with λ′∗=0.049\lambda'^* = 0.049λ′∗=0.049 has standard deviation 5.2×p5.2 \times p5.2×p.

Ex: X∼N(0,1)X \sim N(0, 1)X∼N(0,1). Estimate p=P(10<X<11)p = P(10 < X < 11)p=P(10<X<11) by simulation. The true value is

p=P(10<X<11)=7.6×10−24(board: ≈10−24, the right order of magnitude).p = P(10 < X < 11) = 7.6 \times 10^{-24} \quad (\text{board: } \approx 10^{-24}, \text{ the right order of magnitude}). p=P(10<X<11)=7.6×10−24(board: ≈10−24, the right order of magnitude).

Monte Carlo simulation: generate X1,…,Xn∼N(0,1)X_1, \dots, X_n \sim N(0, 1)X1​,…,Xn​∼N(0,1). Write the probability as an expectation:

P(10<X<11)=E[I{10<X<11}].P(10 < X < 11) = \mathbf{E}\big[I\{10 < X < 11\}\big] . P(10<X<11)=E[I{10<X<11}].

What is III? The indicator function of an event: I{A}=1I\{A\} = 1I{A}=1 if AAA happens and 000 otherwise. So I{10<X<11}I\{10 < X < 11\}I{10<X<11} is a Bernoulli r.v.: it equals 1 with probability ppp and 0 with probability 1−p1 - p1−p. Hence E[I]=1⋅p+0⋅(1−p)=p\mathbf{E}[I] = 1 \cdot p + 0 \cdot (1 - p) = pE[I]=1⋅p+0⋅(1−p)=p and Var⁡(I)=p(1−p)\operatorname{Var}(I) = p(1 - p)Var(I)=p(1−p). This turns any probability into an expectation, with h(y)=I{10<y<11}h(y) = I\{10 < y < 11\}h(y)=I{10<y<11}. The estimator

μ~(n)=1n∑i=1nI{10<Xi<11}\tilde\mu(n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n I\{10 < X_i < 11\} μ~​(n)=n1​i=1∑n​I{10<Xi​<11}

is the fraction of the XiX_iXi​’s that fall in (10,11)(10, 11)(10,11), and

Var⁡(μ~(n))=p(1−p)n≈10−24n.\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\mu(n)) = \frac{p(1 - p)}{n} \approx \frac{10^{-24}}{n} . Var(μ~​(n))=np(1−p)​≈n10−24​.

A 95% CI for μ=p\mu = pμ=p is

[μ~(n)−1.9610−24n,    μ~(n)+1.9610−24n].\left[\tilde\mu(n) - 1.96\sqrt{\frac{10^{-24}}{n}},\;\; \tilde\mu(n) + 1.96\sqrt{\frac{10^{-24}}{n}}\right]. [μ~​(n)−1.96n10−24​​,μ~​(n)+1.96n10−24​​].

  • n=106n = 10^6n=106: half-width =1.9610−24/106=1.96×10−15= 1.96\sqrt{10^{-24}/10^{6}} = 1.96 \times 10^{-15}=1.9610−24/106​=1.96×10−15, about 10910^9109 times larger than ppp.
  • n=1010n = 10^{10}n=1010: half-width =1.9610−24/1010=1.9610−34=1.96×10−17= 1.96\sqrt{10^{-24}/10^{10}} = 1.96\sqrt{10^{-34}} = 1.96 \times 10^{-17}=1.9610−24/1010​=1.9610−34​=1.96×10−17. This is the 10−1710^{-17}10−17 on the board: the half-width is still about ten million times larger than the true mean.

“Variance is too large compared with the true probability?” Yes, exactly. The variance 10−3410^{-34}10−34 is tiny in absolute terms, but what matters is the error relative to the tiny ppp:

standard deviation of μ~(n)p=p(1−p)/np≈1np.\frac{\text{standard deviation of } \tilde\mu(n)}{p} = \frac{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}{p} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{np}} . pstandard deviation of μ~​(n)​=pp(1−p)/n​​≈np​1​.

For the half-width to be even as small as ppp itself (a 100% error!), we need 1.96/np≤11.96/\sqrt{np} \le 11.96/np​≤1, i.e. n≥1.962/p≈5×1023n \ge 1.96^2/p \approx 5 \times 10^{23}n≥1.962/p≈5×1023 runs. Intuitively: with n=1010n = 10^{10}n=1010 runs, the expected number of XiX_iXi​’s that land in (10,11)(10, 11)(10,11) is np≈10−13np \approx 10^{-13}np≈10−13. In practice no XiX_iXi​ ever lands there, so μ~(n)=0\tilde\mu(n) = 0μ~​(n)=0, the sample variance is 0 too, and the computed CI is [0,0][0, 0][0,0]: a meaningless answer. Crude Monte Carlo cannot see an event that it never generates.

Importance sampling. Sample from g=N(10,1)g = N(10, 1)g=N(10,1) instead, i.e. move the normal density to the interval:

Write ϕ\phiϕ for the N(0,1)N(0, 1)N(0,1) density (=f= f=f) and ϕ10\phi_{10}ϕ10​ for the N(10,1)N(10, 1)N(10,1) density (=g= g=g); “N(0,1)/N(10,1)N(0,1)/N(10,1)N(0,1)/N(10,1)” on the board means the ratio ϕ(x)/ϕ10(x)\phi(x)/\phi_{10}(x)ϕ(x)/ϕ10​(x) of the two densities. Then

μ=P(10<X<11)=E[I{10<X<11}]=∫−∞∞I{10<x<11} ϕ(x)ϕ10(x) ϕ10(x)⏟g(x) dx=Eg ⁣[I{10<X<11} ϕ(X)ϕ10(X)]=Eg ⁣[I{10<X<11} 12π e−X2/212π e−(X−10)2/2]=Eg ⁣[I{10<X<11} e−X2/2+(X−10)2/2]=Eg ⁣[I{10<X<11} e−10X+50].\begin{aligned} \mu = P(10 < X < 11) &= \mathbf{E}\big[I\{10 < X < 11\}\big] \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} I\{10 < x < 11\}\,\frac{\phi(x)}{\phi_{10}(x)}\,\underbrace{\phi_{10}(x)}_{g(x)}\, dx \\ &= \mathbf{E}_g\!\left[I\{10 < X < 11\}\,\frac{\phi(X)}{\phi_{10}(X)}\right] \\ &= \mathbf{E}_g\!\left[I\{10 < X < 11\}\,\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-X^2/2}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-(X-10)^2/2}}\right] \\ &= \mathbf{E}_g\!\left[I\{10 < X < 11\}\, e^{-X^2/2 + (X-10)^2/2}\right] \\ &= \mathbf{E}_g\!\left[I\{10 < X < 11\}\, e^{-10X + 50}\right]. \end{aligned} μ=P(10<X<11)​=E[I{10<X<11}]=∫−∞∞​I{10<x<11}ϕ10​(x)ϕ(x)​g(x)ϕ10​(x)​​dx=Eg​[I{10<X<11}ϕ10​(X)ϕ(X)​]=Eg​​I{10<X<11}2π​1​e−(X−10)2/22π​1​e−X2/2​​=Eg​[I{10<X<11}e−X2/2+(X−10)2/2]=Eg​[I{10<X<11}e−10X+50].​

The 12π\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}2π​1​'s cancel out, and −x22+(x−10)22=−x22+x2−20x+1002=−10x+50-\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{(x - 10)^2}{2} = -\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^2 - 20x + 100}{2} = -10x + 50−2x2​+2(x−10)2​=−2x2​+2x2−20x+100​=−10x+50.

Generate X1,…,Xn∼N(10,1)X_1, \dots, X_n \sim N(10, 1)X1​,…,Xn​∼N(10,1). (The board says N(0,1)N(0, 1)N(0,1), but the samples must come from g=N(10,1)g = N(10, 1)g=N(10,1): that is the whole point.) The estimator is

μ^(n)=1n∑i=1nI{10<Xi<11} e−10Xi+50\hat\mu(n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n I\{10 < X_i < 11\}\, e^{-10X_i + 50} μ^​(n)=n1​i=1∑n​I{10<Xi​<11}e−10Xi​+50

(written μ~(n)\tilde\mu(n)μ~​(n) on the board; I use μ^(n)\hat\mu(n)μ^​(n), as in the general formula above, to keep it apart from the crude estimator μ~(n)\tilde\mu(n)μ~​(n)).

Variance:

Var⁡(μ^(n))=1n(Eg[I2{10<X<11} e−20X+100]−p2)=1n(Eg[I{10<X<11} e−20X+100]−p2)≤1n e−100−1n p2=1n(10−44−10−48)≈1n 10−44.\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu(n)) &= \frac{1}{n}\Big(\mathbf{E}_g\big[I^2\{10 < X < 11\}\, e^{-20X + 100}\big] - p^2\Big) \\ &= \frac{1}{n}\Big(\mathbf{E}_g\big[I\{10 < X < 11\}\, e^{-20X + 100}\big] - p^2\Big) \\ &\le \frac{1}{n}\, e^{-100} - \frac{1}{n}\, p^2 = \frac{1}{n}\big(10^{-44} - 10^{-48}\big) \approx \frac{1}{n}\, 10^{-44} . \end{aligned} Var(μ^​(n))​=n1​(Eg​[I2{10<X<11}e−20X+100]−p2)=n1​(Eg​[I{10<X<11}e−20X+100]−p2)≤n1​e−100−n1​p2=n1​(10−44−10−48)≈n1​10−44.​

Step by step:

  1. This is the general formula 1n(Eg[(weighted observation)2]−μ2)\frac{1}{n}\big(\mathbf{E}_g[(\text{weighted observation})^2] - \mu^2\big)n1​(Eg​[(weighted observation)2]−μ2), and the square of the weight is (e−10x+50)2=e−20x+100(e^{-10x + 50})^2 = e^{-20x + 100}(e−10x+50)2=e−20x+100.
  2. I2=II^2 = II2=I, because 02=00^2 = 002=0 and 12=11^2 = 112=1.
  3. The bound: the indicator is nonzero only when 10<X<1110 < X < 1110<X<11, and there −20X+100<−200+100=−100-20X + 100 < -200 + 100 = -100−20X+100<−200+100=−100. So I{10<X<11} e−20X+100≤e−100I\{10 < X < 11\}\, e^{-20X + 100} \le e^{-100}I{10<X<11}e−20X+100≤e−100 always, and its expectation is ≤e−100=3.7×10−44≈10−44\le e^{-100} = 3.7 \times 10^{-44} \approx 10^{-44}≤e−100=3.7×10−44≈10−44.
  4. p2≈(10−24)2=10−48p^2 \approx (10^{-24})^2 = 10^{-48}p2≈(10−24)2=10−48 (with the exact ppp, 5.8×10−475.8 \times 10^{-47}5.8×10−47), negligible.

Compare with crude Monte Carlo:

Var⁡(μ~(n))≈10−24nvs.Var⁡(μ^(n))≲10−44n:\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\mu(n)) \approx \frac{10^{-24}}{n} \qquad\text{vs.}\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu(n)) \lesssim \frac{10^{-44}}{n} : Var(μ~​(n))≈n10−24​vs.Var(μ^​(n))≲n10−44​:

the variance is about 102010^{20}1020 times smaller, for the same nnn. In relative terms, the standard deviation of one sample is now at most 10−44/10−24=100\sqrt{10^{-44}}/10^{-24} = 10010−44​/10−24=100 times ppp (bound with p≈10−24p \approx 10^{-24}p≈10−24), instead of 1/p≈10121/\sqrt p \approx 10^{12}1/p​≈1012 times ppp. E.g. with n=106n = 10^6n=106 the 95% half-width is at most 1.9610−44/106≈2×10−251.96\sqrt{10^{-44}/10^{6}} \approx 2 \times 10^{-25}1.9610−44/106​≈2×10−25, a fraction of ppp, while crude Monte Carlo gave 2×10−152 \times 10^{-15}2×10−15 with the same nnn.

The bound is conservative. The exact per-sample variance is 6.8×10−466.8 \times 10^{-46}6.8×10−46 (computed numerically), i.e. a standard deviation of 3.4×p3.4 \times p3.4×p. E.g. with n=104n = 10^4n=104: 3421 of the XiX_iXi​’s land in (10,11)(10, 11)(10,11), μ^=7.44×10−24\hat\mu = 7.44 \times 10^{-24}μ^​=7.44×10−24, half-width 5.0×10−255.0 \times 10^{-25}5.0×10−25, so the 95% CI is [6.94, 7.95]×10−24[6.94,\ 7.95] \times 10^{-24}[6.94, 7.95]×10−24, which covers p=7.62×10−24p = 7.62 \times 10^{-24}p=7.62×10−24. Over 2000 repetitions, this CI covered ppp in 94.3% of cases.

Why it works: under ggg, about 34% of the XiX_iXi​’s land in (10,11)(10, 11)(10,11) (P(10<X<11)=Φ(1)−Φ(0)=0.341P(10 < X < 11) = \Phi(1) - \Phi(0) = 0.341P(10<X<11)=Φ(1)−Φ(0)=0.341 for X∼N(10,1)X \sim N(10, 1)X∼N(10,1)), instead of np≈10−13np \approx 10^{-13}np≈10−13 expected hits with crude sampling. Each hit is then multiplied by the likelihood ratio e−10x+50e^{-10x + 50}e−10x+50, between e−60=8.8×10−27e^{-60} = 8.8 \times 10^{-27}e−60=8.8×10−27 (at x=11x = 11x=11) and e−50=1.9×10−22e^{-50} = 1.9 \times 10^{-22}e−50=1.9×10−22 (at x=10x = 10x=10), which scales the frequent hits back down to the true, tiny probability.

Choice of the shift: among g=N(θ,1)g = N(\theta, 1)g=N(θ,1), the variance is smallest at θ≈10.05\theta \approx 10.05θ≈10.05 (3.43×p3.43 \times p3.43×p), so θ=10\theta = 10θ=10 is essentially optimal (θ=10.5\theta = 10.5θ=10.5 gives 3.6×p3.6 \times p3.6×p, θ=11\theta = 11θ=11 gives 4.4×p4.4 \times p4.4×p). The reason: fff falls so fast that almost all of the probability of (10,11)(10, 11)(10,11) sits just above 10, i.e. h⋅fh \cdot fh⋅f is concentrated near 10, and the guideline “ggg roughly proportional to h⋅fh \cdot fh⋅f” says to put the samples there.
